In [[theoretical computer science]], specifically in [[term rewriting]], '''Newman's lemma''', also commonly called the '''diamond lemma''', is a criterion to prove that an [[abstract rewriting system]] is [[Confluence (abstract rewriting)|confluent]]. It states that [[Confluence (abstract rewriting)#Local confluence|local confluence]] is a sufficient condition for confluence, provided that the system is also [[Abstract rewriting system#Termination and convergence|terminating]]. This is useful since local confluence is usually easier to verify than confluence.

The lemma was originally proved by [[Max Newman]] in 1942.{{r|newman|van-oostrom}} A considerably simpler proof (given below) was proposed by [[Gérard Huet]].{{r|huet}} A number of other proofs exist.{{r|klop}}

== Statement and proof ==

The lemma is purely combinatorial and applies to any relation. Owing to the context where it is commonly applied, it is stated below in the terminology of [[abstract rewriting system]]s (this is simply a set whose elements are called terms, equipped with a relation <math>\to</math> called reduction, and see the corresponding article for definitions of termination, confluence, local confluence and normal forms).

{{Math theorem
| name =Newman's lemma
| note = {{r|trat|terese|harrison|cohn}}
| math_statement =
 If an abstract rewriting system is terminating and locally confluent, then it is confluent, and every term has a ''unique'' normal form.
}}

{{Math proof
| title=Proof
| proof=
Because <math>\to</math> is terminating, we can perform [[well-founded induction]] on <math>u</math> along <math>\to</math>. We prove that every diagram

[[Image:Proof of Newman's lemma (1).svg|center|frameless|upright=0.8|Diagram with arrows <math>u \to^* v, u \to^* w</math> (arrows are dotted to express that they represent sequences of arbitrarily many reduction steps)]]

can be extended to a diagram

[[Image:Proof of Newman's lemma (2).svg|center|frameless|upright=0.8|Diagram with arrows <math>u \to^* v \to^* t, u \to^* w \to^* t</math>]]

where the dotted arrows represent sequences of arbitrarily many reductions by <math>\to</math>.

Base case: If <math>u = v</math> or <math>u = w</math>, this is trivial. 

Inductive step: Otherwise, we have at least one reduction on each side:

[[Image:Proof of Newman's lemma (3).svg|center|frameless|upright=1.5|alt=Diagram with arrows <math>u \to v_0 \to^* v, u \to w_0 \to^* w</math>]]

By local confluence, this diagram can be extended to:

[[Image:Proof of Newman's lemma (4).svg|center|frameless|upright=1.5|alt=Diagram with arrows <math>u \to v_0 \to^* v, u \to w_0 \to^* w, v_0 \to^* t, w_0 \to^* t</math>]]

then by induction hypothesis on <math>v_0</math>:

[[Image:Proof of Newman's lemma (5).svg|center|frameless|upright=1.5|alt=Diagram with arrows <math>u \to v_0 \to^* v \to^* v_1, u \to w_0 \to^* t \to^* v_1, v_0 \to^* t, w_0 \to^* w</math>]]

and finally, by induction hypothesis on <math>w_0</math>:

[[Image:Proof of Newman's lemma (6).svg|center|frameless|upright=1.5|alt=Diagram with arrows <math>u \to v_0 \to^* v \to^* v_1 \to^* w_1, u \to w_0 \to^* t \to^* v_1, v_0 \to^* t, w_0 \to^* w \to^* w_1</math>]]
}}

== Eriksson's polygon property lemma ==

A related result was shown by Kimmo Eriksson in 1993.{{r|eriksson-thesis|eriksson-journal}}  Recall that an abstract rewriting system is locally confluent if for any two reductions <math>a \to b</math> and <math>a \to c</math>, there exists <math>d</math> such that <math>b \to^* d</math> and <math>c \to^* d</math>.  If additionally it is required that the reduction chains <math>b \to^* d</math> and <math>c \to^* d</math> have the same length, then the system is said to have the '''polygon property'''.  Examples of rewriting systems with the polygon property include [[bubble sort]] and the [[chip-firing game]].

{{Math theorem
| name =Eriksson's polygon property lemma
| note = {{r|eriksson-thesis|eriksson-journal}}  
| math_statement =
If an abstract rewriting system is terminating and has the polygon property, then it is confluent, ''and'' every terminating chain of reductions from a given state has the same length.
}}

{{Math proof
| title=Proof
| proof=
By Newman's lemma, the system is confluent, and every element has a unique normal form. For each element <math>u</math>, define <math>rl(u)</math> be the length of the ''shortest'' reduction chain from <math>u</math> to its normal form.

Induct on <math>rl(u)</math>. If <math>rl(u)=0</math>, then <math>u</math> is already in normal form. Otherwise, <math>rl(u)\geq 1</math>, and we apply the polygonal property and the induction hypothesis.
}}
